title: Non-compete and related agreements: Hoarding talent, holding back growth? (OECD Employment Outlook 2026, chapter)
key_claim: Across 15 OECD countries around one-fifth of private-sector employees are bound by a non-compete clause, 9-16% by training-cost repayment clauses and 10-17% by bonus-repayment clauses; about 40% are covered by an NDA; 5% have been stopped from moving jobs; employers in every country report more increases than decreases in post-employment clause use over five years.
frame_summary: This source is arguing that post-employment restrictions have spread well beyond senior knowledge workers into a layered stack of clauses that measurably slows mobility and productivity, and that policy should treat the stack, not one clause.

title: Opening the door to better and higher paying jobs: banning unfair non-competes (joint media release, Leigh and Rishworth)
date_evidence: Date: 7 September 2026 (page text, joint media release with The Hon Amanda Rishworth MP)
key_claim: On 7 September 2026 the Australian Government released draft legislation banning non-compete clauses for workers under A$190,100 a year, with consultation on co-worker non-solicitation, no-poach and wage-fixing bans, cascading restraints and exemptions to protect legitimate business interests, open until 2 October 2026.
frame_summary: The Australian Government is arguing that non-competes below the high-income threshold hold down wages and productivity and should be banned, while leaving room for exemptions that protect legitimate business interests.
verbatim_quote: ban non‑compete clauses for Australian workers under $190,100 per year
verbatim_list: appropriate exemptions and safeguards to protect legitimate business interests
Submissions can be made online on the Treasury consultation hub until 2 October 2026.

title: The fine print that follows you out the door: non-compete clauses are spreading and holding back growth
date_evidence: July 7, 2026 (modified July 27, 2026); authors Dan Andrews, Andrea Garnero and Sara Holttinen
key_claim: OECD economists report that close to one-half of covered workers receive nothing in return for a non-compete, that NDAs cover around one-half of workers, and that a 10 percentage-point rise in non-compete prevalence is linked to a 1.9% fall in productivity; their survey covered more than 30 000 workers and 6 000 companies.
frame_summary: OECD economists argue that non-competes now bind many workers without confidential knowledge, and without compensation, and that policy options range from earnings-threshold bans to compensation or duration caps.
verbatim_quote: close to one-half of covered workers report receiving nothing at all in return
verbatim_list: more than 30 000 workers and 6 000 companies in all
barring the clauses below an earnings threshold, exempting particular occupations, requiring employers to pay compensation, capping duration, or mandating advance disclosure
notes: Blog companion to the OECD Employment Outlook 2026 chapter; Tier 2 as analytical OECD commentary. Date 'July 7, 2026' read on live page. quote_provenance manually-verified against WebFetch text (two passes).

title: Treasury releases details of proposed ban on post-employment restraints, no-poach arrangements and wage-fixing
key_claim: Allens reads the Australian draft as excluding genuine retention arrangements (deferred bonuses, vesting stock options, service-conditioned leave) and reasonable agreed notice periods and fully paid gardening leave from the non-compete definition.
frame_summary: A law-firm briefing arguing that the draft bans a narrow, defined set of restraints and leaves employers workable alternatives through retention arrangements, notice periods and paid garden leave.
verbatim_quote: Genuine retention arrangements (deferred bonuses, vesting stock options, service-conditioned leave entitlements) are excluded from the non-compete definition.
verbatim_list: Reasonable agreed notice periods and fully paid 'gardening leave' clauses remain outside the relevant definition, provided the employee continues to be paid in full during the restraint.
For the financial year ending 30 June 2027, the high income threshold is $190,100.
notes: Law-firm alert (Tier 3 per sourcing guide). Quotes returned identically across two WebFetch passes; quote_provenance manually-verified. The Allens summary of the draft is secondary to the draft bill itself, which the analyst did not retrieve.

title: Australia: Non-compete reforms, what employers need to know
key_claim: HSF Kramer lists garden leave on full pay, extended-vesting incentive plans, clawbacks and service conditions as tools employers may use instead of non-competes, and warns the reforms could concentrate talent in large businesses.
frame_summary: A law-firm briefing arguing that employers can keep retention protection through deferred compensation and garden leave, and that the reform may produce talent concentration the Government does not intend.
verbatim_quote: Employers may also consider deferred compensation structures, including long-term incentive plans with extended vesting periods, clawback mechanisms and service conditions, as a means of retaining key staff and protecting confidential information.
verbatim_list: This could result in talent concentration in large businesses, which is the opposite of the competitive labour market that the Government intends to foster.
notes: Law-firm alert (Tier 3). quote_provenance manually-verified against two WebFetch passes (the verbatim spans were returned identically on request).

title: Australia: Draft legislation takes hammer to non-competes
key_claim: Baker McKenzie notes that payments which cannot be determined in advance, such as most incentives or commissions, do not count towards the income threshold, and that notice periods are not captured by the legislation.
frame_summary: A law-firm briefing arguing that the draft goes further than expected on restraints but leaves notice periods, garden leave and confidentiality provisions as the practical alternatives for employers.
verbatim_quote: The amount of payments which cannot be determined in advance (e.g., most incentives or commissions) will not be included in this calculation.
verbatim_list: Notice periods are not captured by the legislation.
There is no carve out for high income employees.
notes: Law-firm alert (Tier 3). Date read on live page as '09 September 2026'. quote_provenance manually-verified against WebFetch text (two passes).

title: Government moves to ban non-compete clauses
key_claim: The Tech Council of Australia opposes the ban, arguing non-competes give tech employers an important layer of contractual protection and that even lower-paid staff can access sensitive material; higher-paid tech workers above the threshold would still face non-competes.
frame_summary: Trade press reporting the draft ban through its effect on tech employers, with the industry body arguing that non-competes protect sensitive material even at junior levels.

verbatim_list: one in five Australian workers are subject to a non-compete clause

title: Washington State bans all noncompete agreements effective June 30, 2027
key_claim: Washington's HB 1155 voids all noncompetition covenants from 30 June 2027, regardless of when signed, but allows employers to require repayment of educational expenses if the agreement expires within 18 months, is pro rata and releases employees separated for good cause.
frame_summary: A law-firm briefing arguing that Washington's ban is near-total but leaves training-repayment and narrow non-solicitation arrangements as permitted employer protections.
verbatim_quote: regardless of when they were executed
verbatim_list: limits repayment to the pro rata portion of the remaining time of the 18-month period
expires within 18 months of the employee's start date
